item.title: Navigating regulatory fragmentation in the convergence of synthetic biology, artificial intelligence, and automation
item.description: ## Introduction ### Methodology The analysis focused on four regulatory domains that are increasingly converging in advanced biotechnology research and innovation: biosecurity and biosafety regulation (including pathogen oversight, dual-use research governance, DNA synthesis screening and laboratory biorisk management); artificial intelligence governance (including AI-specific legislation, policy frameworks, standards and regulatory guidance); export control and technology protection regimes (including dual-use controls, technology transfer restrictions, advanced computing controls and research security measures); and data governance and sovereignty requirements.

item.title: Public can testify Monday at AI and data center committee
item.description:
People can share their opinions on data centers and artificial intelligence when a North Dakota legislative committee meets again Monday to address those topics.
The Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee meets at 9 a.m.
The committee, [announced in June](https://northdakotamonitor.com/2026/06/25/north-dakota-lawmakers-zero-in-on-ai-data-centers/), has taken testimony on the pros and cons of artificial intelligence and the impact of data centers that are being built to generate AI.

item.title: From War Booty to War Learning: The Legal Status of Captured Military Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
# From War Booty to War Learning: The Legal Status of Captured Military Artificial Intelligence Unlike traditional military equipment, artificial intelligence is not simply an object whose value lies in its physical characteristics.
Artificial intelligence appears, initially at least, to represent little more than the latest iteration of an established practice.
Artificial intelligence is different.
Artificial intelligence increasingly separates capability from _matériel_ altogether.
Artificial intelligence shifts attention from ownership to learning and places the strategic value of capture less in obtaining an adversary’s hardware than in inheriting years of computational experience and using that experience to accelerate one’s own military development.

item.title: Reviewing Artificial Intelligence in Materials Discovery
item.description:
# Reviewing Artificial Intelligence in Materials Discovery ### Key Takeaways The most recent developments were discussed in a peer-reviewed article published in _Next Materials_.2 The review article focused mostly on how [machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models](https://www.spectroscopyonline.com/view/ai-deep-learning-and-machine-learning-in-the-dynamic-world-of-spectroscopy) are being used to analyze trace evidence such as fibers, paints, glass, soils, polymers, metals, and chemical residues.1 The conclusion is that artificial intelligence (AI) is already having an impact on improving the objectivity of forensic evidence analysis.1
## **How is artificial intelligence (AI) being used in materials science?** These tools include Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), Raman and surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS), gas and liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS/LC–MS), and hyperspectral imaging.1 All these tools have already demonstrated measurable gains in discrimination power, throughput, and objectivity in operational laboratories.1
